meta.title: Who really said "It Seems As If Anything I Like Is Either Illegal, Immoral, or Fattening"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Fields said a version of it in Six of a Kind (1934) — but the line was already in print. The earliest record, from 1933, credits a St. Louis man, Frank Rand.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It Seems As If Anything I Like Is Either Illegal, Immoral, or Fattening'?
meta.ogDescription: Not W. C. Fields, and not quite Alexander Woollcott. The 1933 trail leads to a St. Louis dieter named Frank Rand, and a radio anecdote written down in Albany.

answer.label: Not Alexander Woollcott — first recorded from Frank Rand of St. Louis
answer.authorDates: Dates unknown · St. Louis · quoted on the radio in September 1933
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known record belongs to neither of the men usually credited: on 16 September 1933 the Albany Evening News wrote down an anecdote Alexander Woollcott had just told on his radio show, in which a St. Louis man named Frank Rand, lunching miserably on bouillon cubes and undressed lettuce, delivers the line. Fields spoke a version of it on screen the following February in Paramount’s Six of a Kind, and Quote Investigator ↗ credits the saying to Rand, with Woollcott as its popularizer.

source.excerpt: “Do you eat that stuff because you like it?” someone asked Rand. “No, I hate it,” he replied. “But it seems as if anything I like is either illegal or immoral or fattening.”
trail: 16 September 1933 — The Albany Evening News column “As I Hear It” writes down an anecdote Alexander Woollcott has just told on the radio: Frank Rand of St. Louis, on a punishing diet, says the line. This is the earliest known instance (Quote Investigator ↗).

December 1933 — Reader’s Digest prints the saying over Woollcott’s name with no source given; Rand has disappeared from it. Wikiquote still lists the line among Woollcott’s quotes on that citation (Wikiquote ↗).

9 February 1934 — Paramount releases Six of a Kind, with Fields as Sheriff ‘Honest John’ Hoxley opposite Alison Skipworth (Wikipedia ↗); his version of the retort is transcribed from the scene by Quote Investigator ↗.
7 April 1938 — Walter Winchell notes the credit drifting once more, to a British Consul-General, after years of running as Woollcott’s (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: The columnist — identified by Quote Investigator as Mary A. O’Neill, writing as “The Listener” — was noting down what Woollcott had said on his radio programme. In the setup, Rand is lunching “in the interest of his girth” on bouillon cubes and undressed lettuce. Note the 1933 wording joins the three terms with or; the tidy comma version came later.
source.rightsHolder: Paramount Productions, Inc. and its successors in title (Six of a Kind, 1934); the publisher of the Albany Evening News for the 1933 column
source.rightsNote: This line is not from an old book: its two documented appearances are a newspaper column of 16 September 1933 and a Paramount feature released 9 February 1934, both after the 1931 cut-off for U.S. public domain in 2026, so we treat the sources as in-copyright rather than assert otherwise. Whether a one-sentence quip carries its own protection is a separate question this page does not decide.

author.name: Frank Rand
author.heading: Who was Frank Rand?
author.metaLine: St. Louis, 1933 · the dieter behind the line, known only from Woollcott’s radio anecdote
author.bio: Frank Rand enters the quotation record exactly once: as a St. Louis man grimly lunching on bouillon cubes and undressed lettuce “in the interest of his girth,” whose one-line complaint Alexander Woollcott repeated on the air in September 1933. Quote Investigator credits him with the saying on the strength of that broadcast report — the earliest known instance of it — while noting that Woollcott, not Rand, is the reason the world heard it. Nothing further about him is documented in the sources that trace this line.

copyAttribution: Not Alexander Woollcott, and not W. C. Fields. The earliest known record is a St. Louis man named Frank Rand, quoted on Woollcott's radio show and written down in the Albany Evening News, 16 September 1933: "But it seems as if anything I like is either illegal or immoral or fattening." Fields spoke a version of it on screen in Paramount's Six of a Kind, released 9 February 1934. — quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three claimants, one joke
misattribution.intro: This saying has been pinned on at least three people in its first five years of life. W. C. Fields is the version most people have actually seen — he speaks it on screen in 1934 — but the credit that stuck in print is Alexander Woollcott’s: a December 1933 Reader’s Digest listing that the Yale Book of Quotations, The Quote Verifier and the Dictionary of Modern Proverbs all carried forward (Quote Investigator ↗). Neither man coined it.

items.why: Fields really did say a version of it — on screen in Six of a Kind, released 9 February 1934 by Paramount, where he plays Sheriff ‘Honest John’ Hoxley opposite Alison Skipworth (Wikipedia ↗). Quote Investigator transcribes his retort from the scene, but places it after two 1933 appearances of the joke in print (Quote Investigator ↗). The joke reached the film already made, so it is not a line he coined.

Reader’s Digest printed the saying over Woollcott’s name in December 1933 with no source given, and Wikiquote still lists it among his quotes on that citation (Wikiquote ↗). But the earlier radio report shows him telling it as another man’s remark, and Quote Investigator notes he never claimed to have coined it (Quote Investigator ↗).

By April 1938 Walter Winchell was noting that a newspaper had credited the line to the British Consul-General — “Which is the way we ran it years ago, when it was credited to Alexander Woollcott,” he wrote (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: On current evidence, Quote Investigator ↗ credits the expression to Frank Rand of St. Louis. Woollcott carried it to a national audience; Fields carried it to the movies.

context.heading: Why this one travels
lead: It is a joke about appetite, and appetite is universal — which is exactly why the line refuses to stay attached to anyone. In September 1933 it belonged to a man on a lettuce diet. By December a mass-circulation magazine had reassigned it to the most quotable wit in America. By the following February it was coming out of W. C. Fields’s mouth on a Paramount screen, and by 1938 Walter Winchell was watching a newspaper hand it to a British Consul-General. Nobody was lying; the joke simply travels faster than its provenance.

Fields is where it finally settled, and that is its own kind of evidence. He is one of the great attribution magnets: Wikipedia notes that the famous crack about a man who hates dogs and babies was actually made about Fields by the humorist Leo Rosten at a 1939 testimonial dinner, and was later credited to Fields himself by Bartlett’s (Wikipedia ↗). A gravelly, put-upon delivery is enough to make almost any complaint about pleasure sound like his.
context.detailsSummary: Loose ends: who Rand was, and where else the line surfaced
detailsBody: Who was Frank Rand? Quote Investigator identifies him only as “Mr. Frank Rand of St. Louis.” A prominent St. Louis businessman of that name, Frank C. Rand (1876–1949), ran the International Shoe Company in exactly that period (Wikipedia ↗) — but no source we could fetch connects him to the remark, and this page does not make that identification.

The line kept moving. Quote Investigator records a July 1934 newspaper cartoon caption that carries the joke with no attribution at all, and the fact-check blog Quote/Counterquote notes a further screen version in the 1939 film Love Affair, spoken by Irene Dunne (Quote/Counterquote ↗).
context.pull: Woollcott told it as somebody else’s joke. The world heard it as his — then as Fields’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known instance is the Albany Evening News of 16 September 1933 (p. 14, col. 6), column "As I Hear It" by "The Listener" (identified as Mary A. O'Neill), reporting Woollcott's radio anecdote about Frank Rand of St. Louis: "But it seems as if anything I like is either illegal or immoral or fattening." QI concludes the expression should be credited to Frank Rand, with Woollcott the prime catalyst of its popularity; it also gives the December 1933 Reader's Digest citation, the Six of a Kind (Feb 1934) dialogue with Fields as Sheriff Hoxley and Alison Skipworth, the unattributed July 1934 Girligags cartoon caption, and Walter Winchell's April 1938 note about the British Consul-General credit.
Wikiquote's Alexander Woollcott page lists "All the things I really like to do are either illegal, immoral, or fattening" in its Quotes (sourced) section, cited to Reader's Digest (December 1933).
Wikiquote's W. C. Fields page contains no line about anything being illegal, immoral or fattening, in either its Quotes or Misattributed section, and does not cover Six of a Kind.

Six of a Kind was released 9 February 1934 by Paramount, directed by Leo McCarey, with W. C. Fields as Sheriff 'Honest John' Hoxley and Alison Skipworth as Mrs. K. Rumford. The article does not quote the illegal/immoral/fattening line.

W. C. Fields (born William Claude Dukenfield, 29 January 1880 – 25 December 1946) was an actor and comedian; the remark about a man who hates dogs and babies was made by humorist Leo Rosten at a 1939 testimonial dinner and was later erroneously attributed to Fields by Bartlett's Familiar Quotations.

Quote/Counterquote credits the saying to Alexander Woollcott while noting it does not appear in his written works, cites the December 1933 Reader's Digest listing without a specific source, quotes Fields's version from Six of a Kind (1934), and notes Irene Dunne saying a variant in the 1939 film Love Affair.

Frank C. Rand (1876–1949) was a St. Louis businessman who led the International Shoe Company; the article makes no mention of Woollcott or this saying (cited only for who he was, not for the attribution).
